title: Nun and samech (Berakhot 4b)
hook: nun is missing from Ashrei, but the next verse says God upholds all who fall

segments.voice: Yesterday, mem, the letter of mayim, water. Your line was mem is water. Did the glass of water taste any different when you drank it slowly? Today, two letters that the rabbis read as a pair. Day one thousand three hundred forty-two.

Psalm one hundred forty-five is built like a ladder. Each verse begins with the next letter of the alef-bet: alef, then bet, then gimel, climbing in order. Jews know it as Ashrei, from the words said just before it in the prayer book, and it comes up again and again in the daily services. Say it slowly, letter by letter, and somewhere past the middle you might notice a rung is gone. After mem comes samech. There's no verse for nun. The ladder skips a step. A missing letter in a prayer said that often is the kind of thing the rabbis could not leave alone. Today they ask why.
screen: `A PSALM BUILT LETTER BY LETTER.` → `AFTER MEM, SAMECH.` → `WHERE IS NUN?`

segments.voice: The question is asked in the Talmud, in tractate Berakhot. Why is there no nun in Ashrei? Rabbi Yochanan answers: because a verse that begins with nun tells of Israel's fall. He points to the prophet Amos, whose lament opens with the Hebrew word for fallen, nafelah: the maiden of Israel has fallen, and will not rise again. A psalm of praise, the Talmud suggests, did not want to open a line with that word. But the answer doesn't stop there. Another sage, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, carries it on: even so, David returned and held them up. Look at the very next verse, the samech verse. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation it reads: "The LORD upholdeth all that fall." In Hebrew it begins somech, supporting. Somech Adonai l'chol hanoflim. The Lord supports all the fallen. Turn that over. The verse that lifts begins with samech. And the word it uses for the ones who fell, noflim, comes from the same root as the word Amos used. The fall is not erased from the psalm. It is folded into the next line, already being held. So the empty space where nun should be is not a silence. It's the moment of falling, and the line that catches it is right there beneath. Some readers hear it as a picture of how a fall is meant to work in a community: nobody pretends it didn't happen, and nobody leaves the one who fell lying on the ground. The nun falls. The samech is already reaching out. And it all happens inside a psalm said on an ordinary morning, before the rest of the day begins.
screen: `WHY NO NUN? THE TALMUD ASKS.` · `AMOS: FALLEN, AND WILL NOT RISE.` · `THE NEXT VERSE: GOD UPHOLDS THE FALLEN.` · `THE FALL IS HELD, NOT ERASED.` · then, large: `THE LORD UPHOLDETH ALL THAT FALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lift someone who fell. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who has stumbled lately. A friend who lost a job, a child who failed a test, a coworker who made a public mistake, maybe you. Don't fix it yet. Just notice where they are: on the ground, or halfway up. Then choose one small way to be the next line under them. A message, a coffee, a word that says the fall isn't the whole story. If you pray, you can say the samech verse quietly. The bell holds the time.
Nun and samech. Nun, the missing rung in Ashrei, the letter of falling. Samech, the letter of the verse that holds up all who fall. Today's word.
Your line: nun falls, samech lifts. Today, send the message or make the call to the one you thought of, before evening. Day one thousand three hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Psalm 145, called Ashrei, is part of the daily Jewish prayer services; its verses follow the alef-bet, and the Talmud in Berakhot 4b explains the missing nun verse by pointing to the samech verse that follows.

fork.setup: you're compiling a psalm of praise, letter by letter. the only nun line you can think of is about falling and never rising. what do you do?
options: write the fall in anyway, right where it goes.
leave nun out, and let the next verse hold up the fallen.
fork.reveal: the Talmud's answer: no nun verse, and the samech verse that follows says God upholds all who fall. the fall is held, not erased.

original.note: Hebrew: supporting, holding up — the first word of the samech verse in Ashrei.

trapdoor: what you thought: an alphabet psalm with a typo.
what it means: nun is left out, and the samech verse right after it says God upholds all who fall.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 4b — Rabbi Yochanan reads the gap through Amos 5:2, and the next verse, Psalm 145:14, as David lifting them back up.

sources.quoted: The LORD upholdeth all that fall

notes: Psalm 145:14 fragment quoted as JPS 1917; KJV has the same words for this fragment. Confirm.
Amos 5:2 paraphrased; Berakhot 4b (Rabbi Yochanan's explanation and 'David returned and supported them') paraphrased. Confirm attribution to Rabbi Yochanan.

Ashrei's name explained as coming from the verses said before Psalm 145 (Psalms 84:5, 144:15); 'comes up again and again in the daily services' kept general under the claims rule (Berakhot 4b mentions saying it three times daily). Confirm.
The claim that noflim and Amos's nafelah share a root (n-f-l) is standard Hebrew grammar; confirm.
Deliberately omitted: the Dead Sea Psalms scroll that includes a nun verse (a manuscript claim). A Keeper may want it mentioned.

Editor: 'David returned and held them up' now attributed to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak (Berakhot 4b gives it to him, not Rabbi Yochanan); cut 'between breakfast and the rest of the day', since the morning service is traditionally said before eating.
